# Exam Pattern - BIM 8th Semester (TU, Faculty of Management)

> **Sources of truth:** the official **TU/FOM model question set 2026** (Dean's Office PDF, saved in `_raw/pdf/`) and the **2026 board papers** as published. Every row below is confirmed on at least two of: model question, board paper, syllabus.
>
> **Corrected 2026-11-18.** Earlier versions of this file said all four subjects were 60/30 with a 10 × 1 Group A. That was true of Business Intelligence only, and it was generalised too fast. Two of the four papers are **100 marks**, and their Group A carries 2 marks per question.

## There are two paper sizes

| | **Pattern A — 60 marks** | **Pattern B — 100 marks** |
|---|---|---|
| **Subjects** | IT 249 Business Intelligence · IT 277 Cloud Computing | IT 248 IT Entrepreneurship & Management · IT 250 Digital Economy |
| Full / pass marks | **60 / 30** | **100 / 50** |
| Time | 3 hours | 3 hours |
| Group A | 10 × **1** = 10, all compulsory | 10 × **2** = 20, all compulsory |
| Group B | any **5 of 6** × **3** = 15 | any **6 of 7** × **5** = 30 |
| Group C | any **3 of 4** × **5** = 15 | any **3 of 4** × **10** = 30 |
| Group D | 1 × 20 (board 2026) or 2 × 10 (model) = 20 | 1 × 20 = 20 |
| Attempted if you answer everything | 68 → 60 counted | 115 → 100 counted |

### The same paper, twice as much writing

Pattern B asks for **40 more marks in the same 180 minutes**. That is not a detail — it changes how you prepare:

- Group A in a 100-mark paper is **20 marks of short definitions**, not 10. Ten 2-markers at 50-60 words each is a page and a half before you reach Group B.
- Group C is **10 marks per question**, not 5. A 10-mark answer is a structured argument (~350-400 words) with a worked example, not five bullet points.
- The safety margin is thinner: Pattern B's Group B offers 7 questions and you need 6, so only **one** topic can be dropped. Pattern A lets you drop one of six.

## What a Group D answer must contain (both patterns)

20 marks for one case with 3-4 sub-questions. Nobody passes comfortably without attempting it properly.

The method, unchanged across subjects and across both shapes:

1. **One line restating the case** — proves you read it, costs 15 seconds.
2. **Each sub-question under its own heading**, in the paper's order, with the mark weight in mind (5-mark sub-question ≈ 180-220 words).
3. **Course concepts named explicitly** — a case answer without the subject's vocabulary is a newspaper column.
4. **A recommendation or judgement at the end** — the marks for "evaluate" and "suggest" live there.

⚠ **Two Group D shapes are both live.** The 2026 board paper used **1 × 20** (one company, four sub-parts). The 2026 model question for IT 249 and IT 277 used **2 × 10** (two shorter cases, no choice). Rehearse both: one deep case and two shallow ones in the same 55 minutes.

## Strategic reading of each group

1. **Group A is the cheapest marks on the paper — and the easiest to lose.** Every 1- or 2-marker is a definition or a two-item list. If a definition is on the syllabus, it is a probable Group A question. Every unit file therefore opens with the definition in write-ready form.
2. **Group B is the safety net.** You always get one more question than you need. Breadth beats depth; know the shape of every topic rather than the detail of one.
3. **Group C is where diagrams and comparisons pay.** Across the model questions, Group C is dominated by four archetypes: **architecture** (draw and label), **process** (steps in order), **comparison** (two things against each other, with strengths and weaknesses), and **design/apply** (build something for a stated business). If an answer has no diagram, no steps and no comparison, it is probably a 3-mark answer wearing a 5-mark label.
4. **Group D is a third to a fifth of the paper and it is compulsory.** It is also the only place where a prepared skeleton transfers across subjects almost unchanged.

## Answer-length discipline

| Marks | Target | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ≤ 30 words | definition or one reason. No intro. |
| 2 | 45-60 words | definition + one sentence of substance, or two named items with a half-line each |
| 3 | 80-120 words | 3 named points, or point + 2 lines of support |
| 5 | 180-250 words | intro line → 4-5 points or labelled diagram → closing line |
| 10 | 330-420 words | 4-6 headed points, one worked example, a judgement |
| 20 | 600-800 words | per sub-question headings, concepts named, recommendation at the end |

## Exam-hall timing

**Pattern A — 60 marks (IT 249, IT 277)**

| Phase | Minutes |
|---|---|
| Group A (10 × 1) | 20 |
| Group B (5 × 3) | 40 |
| Group C (3 × 5) | 50 |
| Group D (20) | 55 |
| Review + diagram finishing | 15 |

**Pattern B — 100 marks (IT 248, IT 250)**

| Phase | Minutes |
|---|---|
| Group A (10 × 2) | 25 |
| Group B (6 × 5) | 45 |
| Group C (3 × 10) | 60 |
| Group D (20) | 45 |
| Review + diagram finishing | 5 |

In both papers: **write Group D's outline first**, even though you answer it last. The case then turns over in your head while you write the short answers — and you will not run out of time having spent everything on Group A.

In Pattern B the review buffer is deliberately only 5 minutes. There is no slack in a 100-mark paper; the discipline is to finish each question inside its slot, not to check at the end.

## Verified vs unverified

- ✅ **IT 249** — 60/30, 10 × 1 / 5 × 3 / 3 × 5 / 1 × 20: read directly from the 2026 board paper, and independently confirmed by the official model question (which prints 60/30 with the same A/B/C split and a 2 × 10 Group D).
- ✅ **IT 277** — 60/30, same split: official model question only. No board paper exists.
- ✅ **IT 248** — 100/50, 10 × 2 / 6 × 5 / 3 × 10 / 1 × 20: 2026 board paper *and* official model question agree.
- ✅ **IT 250** — 100/50, same split: 2026 board paper prints the figures and its mark tags sum to 115 attempted → 100 counted. **No model question exists for this subject** (verified absent from the FOM 2026 set) — see `02-digital-economy/model-question.md`.
- ⚠ **Group D's exact shape varies** between board paper and model question. Both are rehearsed; neither is assumed.
